claims.text: In single-phase high-entropy superconducting alloys, Tc is governed primarily by effective electron–phonon coupling.
The effective electron–phonon coupling is modulated by local lattice distortions arising from a broad distribution of atomic masses and sizes.
Reducing the variance in local lattice strain will narrow the phonon density-of-states distribution.
Reducing local-strain variance through controlled substitution will increase Tc relative to the unmodified alloy.
The proposed starting material is a disordered, single-phase solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each.
The proposed starting alloy is based on heavy transition metals outside the best-studied Nb–Ta and titanium-rich systems.
Replacing a constituent with an element of similar valence but closer-to-average atomic mass and size will reduce local lattice strain.
The proposed substitution will narrow the spread of the phonon spectrum without significantly altering electron count.
High-temperature homogenization followed by annealing will produce a single-phase solid solution with reduced residual stress.
Dispersions in atomic sizes and masses create local lattice distortions and strain fields.
Local lattice distortions and strain fields create a broad, multimodal phonon spectrum.
These phonon-spectrum inhomogeneities mediate the electron–phonon coupling responsible for superconducting pairing.
A broad distribution of vibrational modes weakens effective electron–phonon coupling by dispersing the phonon modes.
Reduced lattice strain concentrates phonon spectral weight at frequencies more favorable for Cooper pairing.
Concentrating phonon spectral weight at favorable frequencies enhances Tc.
The modified alloy will have a higher Tc than the baseline alloy.
The modified alloy will have a sharper resistive and magnetic superconducting transition than the baseline alloy.
The modified alloy will have lower residual resistivity because it has less scattering from lattice irregularities.

The mechanism applies only to single-phase, disordered high-entropy alloys lacking long-range order and may fail if substitution changes carrier density, induces phase separation, or induces ordering.
Failure of the modified alloy to show a statistically significant Tc increase and a sharper transition with lower residual resistivity would falsify the proposed strain–electron–phonon mechanism.
